'''William E. Moffitt''' (9 November 1925 – 19 December 1958<ref>[https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1959/1/5/moffitt-dies-in-gym-from-heart/ The Harvard Crimson, 5 January 1959]</ref>) was a British [[quantum chemist]]. He died after a heart attack following a [[Squash (sport)|squash]] match.<ref name="timesobit">Prof William Moffit, Obituaries, by [[Charles Coulson]], The Times, 30 December 1958 page 8</ref> He had been thought to be one of Britain's most gifted academics.<ref name="nature">{{cite journal |first=Edgar Bright|last=Wilson | title = Prof. William Moffitt | journal = Nature | volume = 184 | pages = 21–22 | year = 1959 | doi = 10.1038/184021b0 | issue=4679|bibcode = 1959Natur.184...21W | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Early life==
Moffitt was born in [[Berlin]], [[Germany]] to [[British people|British]] parents; his father was working in Berlin on behalf of the British government.<ref name="nature" /> He was educated by private tuition up to the age of 11.<ref name="nature" /> He attended [[Harrow School]] from 1936–43. His chemistry master later said of him that "he was undoubtably the most able of a decade of gifted boys ... [and] has a profound effect on all who met him. He did more than anyone to create in the school the intellectual climate so necessary for the stimulation of young minds".<ref name="timesobit" />

==Academic career==
He then studied chemistry at [[New College, Oxford]], under an open scholarship, and graduated with first class honours. His D.Phil. supervisor, [[Charles Coulson]], later wrote:
<blockquote>[his] exuberant delight in life remained with him to the end. "Moffit's method of Atoms in Molecules" will remain for many years to remind us of his remarkable ability to initiate new ways of thinking in his professional subject.</blockquote>

After receiving his D.Phil. for research in [[quantum chemistry]], he joined the research staff of the [[British Rubber Producers Research Association]].<ref name="timesobit" />

He was made an assistant professor at [[Harvard]] in January 1953,<ref name="nature" /> and was give an A.M Honoris Causa in 1955.<ref name="timesobit" /> His colleague [[Edgar Bright Wilson]] said:

<blockquote>Few men had as great an impact at so early an age. The reasons are clear. Few have been endowed with such a sparkling, quick and keen intelligence, with such a capacity for spending long hours in the thorough study of fundamental subjects ... His intellectual powers were not only applied to the solution of problems but perhaps even more to their wise selection. He avoided areas where only formal solutions were attainable, with no contact with experience.<ref name="nature" /></blockquote>

[[Doctorate|Doctoral]] students who were advised by Moffitt include [[R. Stephen Berry]] and [[S. M. Blinder]].<ref>[https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=54102 ChemistryTree: William E. Moffitt]</ref>

==Personal life and interests==
He married Dorothy Silberman in 1956 and had a daughter, Alison in June 1958.<ref name="nature" /> He was a keen rugby player and enjoyed music and arts<ref name="timesobit"/> and particularly English literature.<ref name="nature"/> While sharing a cabin with a monk on a voyage to the UK from the US, he discussed the philosophy of religion with him in their only common language, Latin.<ref name="timesobit"/>
